_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 8 Presenting Data. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (the table; the graph; building it; solving a problem; data at work), with the lesson's own 'Paper, or computer?' step for 2MD.01. EVERY NUMBER IN EVERY PICTURE IS DRAWN FROM ONE COPY OF THE LESSON'S OWN DATA: the party survey (apple 2, banana 4, orange 1, grapes 1) and PLAYGROUND (Monday 9, Tuesday 4, Wednesday 7, Thursday 3, Friday 8), so a column is as many blocks as the table says and the spoken number is the same number. Which fruit won and which day is busiest or quietest are decided by the kit's own ART.sortRows rather than retyped.
title: Presenting Data
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Know how to use computing devices to present categorical data.
Understand how data may help to solve problems.
Know the advantages of storing data and information on computers.

beats.say: Apple two. Banana four. Orange one. Grapes one. Which fruit did most children choose?

at.ask: Which fruit did most children choose

beats.say: Draw those four numbers as columns, and you can see the answer at a glance.

at.draw: Draw those four numbers as columns

beats.say: Your class answered a survey about party fruit. The answers went into a table.
A table holds the numbers in rows. Apple two. Banana four.
Orange one. Grapes one. Every number in the table is exact.
To find the winner you have to read every single number.
A block graph shows the same data as columns.
One column for each fruit. One block for each answer.
Banana is the tallest column, so banana is the answer.
You saw it before you read a single number.
The graph holds no more data than the table. It just makes it easy to see.

at.same: no more data than the table

beats.say: The computer builds the graph from the table, column by column.
Apple two: two blocks. Banana four: four blocks.
Orange one block. Grapes one block. Every column is built.
A column stops when it has as many blocks as the table says.

at.many: as many blocks as the table says

beats.say: Now the pattern shows itself, and the tallest column wins.
The playground is too crowded. That is a problem.
So the class counted the children playing football each day.
Monday nine. Tuesday four. Wednesday seven. Thursday three. Friday eight.
Monday has nine. That is the biggest number in the table.
Thursday has three. That is the smallest number.
So football club moves to Thursday. Read the data, then decide.
Grown-ups solve problems with data every day.
A shop counts what sells. Bananas sell out, so it orders more.
A doctor charts a temperature. A city counts cars before building a crossing.
A school kitchen counts lunches, so it cooks the right amount.
Why keep the class data on a computer, not on paper?
The paper list got wet. The copy on the computer is still there.
Find one name out of five hundred? The computer searches it in a blink.

at.find: Find one name out of five hundred

beats.say: It copies the table, sends it, and draws the graph in a blink.
A table holds the numbers. A graph shows them as columns.

at.graph: A graph shows them as columns

beats.say: The tallest column is the most, and you see it at a glance.

at.tallest: The tallest column is the most

beats.say: Read the data first, then decide. That is solving a problem.
And a computer keeps it safe, and draws the graph.
